label: The Trifocal Tensor
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 365 to 390 and introduces the trifocal tensor as the three-view analogue of the fundamental matrix. Emphasise that it is a single homogeneous object with eighteen degrees of freedom that ties together the geometry of three cameras, governing line and point transfer between the views.

label: From Two Views to Three
notes: Remind students that the fundamental matrix encodes pairwise epipolar geometry but cannot transfer a point uniquely. With three views the constraints become richer: corresponding features satisfy trilinear relations. Stress that the trifocal tensor captures exactly the part of three-view geometry that is independent of scene structure.

label: Canonical Cameras and Definition
notes: Work through the canonical frame where the first camera is the identity projection. Show that the tensor slices are differences of outer products formed from the columns of the second and third camera matrices. Make clear the index convention: the slice index belongs to view one, rows to view two, columns to view three.

label: Line-Triplet Incidence
notes: Explain that each image line back-projects to a plane through its camera centre, and three corresponding lines must share one space line. Derive the point-line-line relation: contracting the tensor with the two image lines reproduces the line in the first view up to scale. This incidence is what creates the tensor.

label: Tensor Slices and Rank
notes: Each slice is a rank-two matrix because it is a difference of two outer products. Its left null-vector is an epipolar line in view two and its right null-vector an epipolar line in view three. Have students compute slice ranks numerically and confirm the null-vectors directly from the singular value decomposition.

label: Epipoles and Fundamental Matrices
notes: The null-lines of the three slices meet at the epipoles of the first camera seen in views two and three. Once those epipoles are recovered, the tensor yields the two fundamental matrices relating the first view to the others. Stress that pairwise fundamentals are shadows of the fuller three-view geometry.

label: Plane-Induced Homographies
notes: Contracting the tensor with a line in the second view produces a homography from view one to view three. Geometrically the line selects a plane through the second camera centre, and that plane induces the point-to-point map. This is the engine behind tensor-based point transfer, so make the construction explicit.

label: Point Transfer
notes: Show how a correspondence between views one and two predicts the third image. Choose a non-epipolar line through the second-view point, build the induced homography, and map the first-view point. Contrast this with intersecting two epipolar lines, which is the pairwise alternative students already know from earlier chapters.

label: Transfer Stability
notes: Pairwise epipolar transfer intersects two lines in the third image and degenerates when those lines are nearly parallel, which happens near the trifocal plane through the three centres. Tensor transfer avoids that collapse. Walk through the error-versus-offset curve so students see the conditioning advantage quantitatively, not just conceptually.

label: Choosing the Transfer Line
notes: Warn that the line through the second-view point must not be the epipolar line. For an exact correspondence any other line gives the same transferred point, but the epipolar choice sends the transfer vector to zero and leaves the homogeneous point undefined. This is the practical caveat behind tensor point transfer.

label: Trilinear Constraints
notes: Present the point-point-point relation as an executable incidence test built from the two skew-symmetric point matrices and the contracted tensor. For a consistent triple all nine entries vanish to roundoff; perturbing one view leaves a structured residual signature. These trilinearities are the algebraic heart of three-view matching.

label: Constraints and Takeaways
notes: Close by noting the tensor has twenty-seven entries but only eighteen degrees of freedom, so a valid tensor must satisfy internal constraints. Recap that it is homogeneous and projectively invariant, unifies line and point transfer, and exposes the epipoles and fundamental matrices of the triple.
